query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Interface doping of the internal boundaries in eutectic high-entropy alloys will enhance both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility by increasing boundary cohesion and suppressing microcrack nucleation.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies having numerous internal boundaries that serve as sites for microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted interface doping treatment—by adding a minor amount of a dopant element that preferentially segregates to internal boundaries during a controlled annealing process—to modify the interfacial chemistry without disrupting the lamellar architecture.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation; dopant concentration and thermal-mechanical processing parameters are optimized to promote interfacial segregation while maintaining the existing dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemically modified internal boundaries with enhanced cohesion and reduced energy states.
generation.mechanism: The dopant atoms segregate to the internal boundaries, reducing the local boundary energy and strengthening the interfacial bonds. This reduction in interfacial weakness delays or prevents microcrack nucleation and propagation under tensile stress, thereby simultaneously improving strength (via better load transfer) and ductility (via delayed crack growth).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy baseline, the interface-doped alloy would exhibit an increase in both tensile strength and room-temperature ductility, as microcrack initiation at internal boundaries is suppressed.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy processed by conventional methods, in which numerous internal boundaries promote premature microcracking leading to limited tensile ductility despite relatively high strength.
generation.boundary: The improvement is contingent upon selecting a dopant that segregates to the internal boundaries without forming deleterious phases and optimizing the doping level and thermal treatment; excessive doping or inappropriate processing could potentially lead to embrittlement or an altered lamellar morphology.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dopant type, its concentration, and the precise thermal-mechanical processing conditions required for effective segregation are not fully defined. Additionally, there is uncertainty whether the interface modification will simultaneously enhance both properties without introducing other adverse effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition: one set to receive the interface doping treatment with the selected dopant and controlled annealing profile, and a control set processed by conventional methods. Conduct detailed microstructural analyses (via TEM and atom probe tomography) to confirm dopant segregation at internal boundaries. Then perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both sets.
measurements: Tensile strength and strain-to-failure under room-temperature loading
Quantitative analysis of dopant concentration at internal boundaries using atom probe or TEM-EDS
Fractography to assess microcrack initiation and propagation
Comparative stress–strain curves between treated and untreated specimens
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the interface-doped specimens do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the control, or if microstructural analysis fails to show robust dopant segregation at the internal boundaries, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] . HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in th

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
